The Quiet Return of the Honeybee

By Lena Ortiz · April 12, 2026

Share on Facebook Tweet Email

After more than a decade of alarming losses, honeybee colonies across North America are showing a strong recovery, according to a survey released this week by the Pollinator Research Council. Beekeepers reported winter losses of 18 percent, the lowest figure since the survey began in 2007.

Researchers credit the turnaround to a combination of better mite control, more diverse forage, and changes in pesticide use. The varroa mite, a parasite that spreads viruses between bees, had been the single largest driver of colony collapse, and new treatments have cut infestation rates by nearly half.

Why the varroa mite mattered

The varroa mite feeds on the fat bodies of developing bees, weakening their immune systems. Colonies with heavy infestations often fail during winter, when bees cannot forage and must survive on stored honey. Dr. Amara Singh, an entomologist at the University of Guelph, said that controlling mites in late summer is the most important step a beekeeper can take.

"If you get the mites under control before the winter bees are born, the colony has a real chance," Singh said. "Most of the losses we saw in the past decade came from mites, not from a mysterious disease."

Forage and farming

Farmers have also played a role. Programs that pay landowners to plant wildflower strips along field edges have expanded to more than two million acres. These strips give bees a varied diet throughout the season, which strengthens colonies and helps them resist disease.

  • Wildflower strips now cover more than two million acres of farmland.
  • Restrictions on neonicotinoid pesticides took effect in several states in 2021.
  • Mite treatments based on oxalic acid became widely available to hobbyists.

What comes next

Not every pollinator is doing as well. Wild bumblebee populations continue to decline, and scientists warn that the recovery of managed honeybees should not distract from the needs of native species. The council plans to expand its survey next year to include wild bees for the first time.

For beekeepers, the message is cautious optimism. Weather, new pests and economic pressures could reverse the gains, but the past three years show that coordinated action can make a measurable difference.
